terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation; dē and the ablative for the subject, cum and the ablative for the person
evidence: Cic. Att. 3.9.2: sed tēcum haec omnia cōram agēmus
Traupman 97: cōram id agere possumus, we can discuss that face to face
Traupman p. 105: we can discuss that one on one, id cōram agere possumus
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: agere cum aliquō dē aliquā rē, “to treat, deal, negotiate, confer, talk with one about a person or thing”. Cicero ends letters with cētera cōram, “the rest when we meet”.

evidence: Traupman 26, 29: Disputābimus dē illā rē crās
Cic. Rep. 1.10 (Lewis & Short): dē mōribus, dē virtūtibus, dē rē pūblicā
terms.comment: With dē and the ablative; Lewis & Short: to discuss a doubtful subject, “very freq. in Cicero’s philos. and rhet. writings”. Traupman’s word for “discuss”.

evidence: Cic. Lael. 33: quae saepissimē inter mē et Scīpiōnem dē amīcitiā disserēbantur
terms.comment: Of setting out a subject in a long talk.

evidence: Cic. Off. 1.7: omnis disputātiō dē officiō futūra est
terms.comment: For a chat rather than a discussion, sermō (see talk).

phrases.latin: advolā ad nōs eō animō ut nōs amēs, tē amārī sciās. cētera cōram agēmus.
phrases.english: Hurry to us, ready to love us and sure that you are loved. We’ll discuss the rest in person.

phrases.latin: sīn es in viā, cum eris mē adsecūtus, cōram agēmus quae erunt agenda.
phrases.english: But if you’re on the road, we’ll discuss what needs discussing in person, once you’ve caught up with me.
We can discuss that face to face.
